classification.difficultyReason: Apply the distance formula to labelled endpoints, including horizontal and vertical intervals.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess endpoint distance; horizontal and vertical intervals are special cases of the taught formula.
questions.methodNote: The derivation and Example 1 calculate the squared distance from coordinate differences, then take the positive square root. The summary repeats this formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the distance formula to labelled endpoints, including horizontal and vertical intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the distance formula to integer coordinates, including negative coordinates and simplified surds.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the six parts directly assesses distance between two specified points using the method in Example 1; no midpoint or gradient calculation is required.
questions.methodNote: The distance formula is derived using Pythagoras. Example 1 substitutes coordinate differences into AB squared, evaluates the squares, then takes the positive square root and simplifies surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the distance formula to integer coordinates, including negative coordinates and simplified surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into the midpoint formula, including negative coordinates and fractional results.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply the midpoint formula to two supplied endpoints, following Example 2.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives the midpoint by averaging corresponding coordinates. Page 4 Example 2 calculates the x- and y-coordinates separately and states the resulting ordered pair.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into the midpoint formula, including negative coordinates and fractional results.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine midpoint and distance calculations, then establish equal sides to classify a triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly apply the midpoint and distance formulas. Part c applies the distance formula to the remaining side and uses equal side lengths to identify an isosceles triangle.
questions.methodNote: Average the endpoint coordinates to find the midpoint, as in Example 2. Calculate squared distances from coordinate differences and then take the positive square root, as in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine midpoint and distance calculations, then establish equal sides to classify a triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the distance formula, retain both square-root signs, and draw the two possible endpoints. These are familiar linked operations.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts reverse the distance calculations demonstrated in Example 1. Parts b and c additionally require plotting the two possible endpoints. The midpoint teaching on pages 3 and 4 is not needed.
questions.methodNote: Use the squared distance formula derived from Pythagoras, substitute coordinate differences, and solve for the unknown coordinate. Retain both square-root signs when the squared difference is positive.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange the squared distance formula to find unknown coordinates, retaining both possible values and illustrating them.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine distance and midpoint calculations to find lengths within a triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply the two formulas directly. Part c combines the midpoint result with equal half-interval lengths and a further distance calculation.
questions.methodNote: Use squared coordinate differences and Pythagoras to calculate distances, then take the positive square root. Average corresponding coordinates to find a midpoint; a midpoint divides its interval into equal halves.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine distance and midpoint calculations to find lengths within a triangle.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the midpoint formula to find an unknown endpoint in each part.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess reversing the midpoint formula. The supplied reuse candidates have different tasks and coordinates, so neither is source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives each midpoint coordinate as the average of the corresponding endpoint coordinates; page 4 Example 2 substitutes coordinates into those averages. Apply the same formula and solve for each unknown endpoint coordinate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse the midpoint formula to find an unknown endpoint in each part.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate squared side lengths and use the converse of Pythagoras’ theorem to establish a right angle.

questions.mappingNote: Use the taught squared-distance calculations for the three sides, then apply the converse of Pythagoras’ theorem to prove the requested triangle property. Neither supplied reuse candidate has these vertices and this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 derives distance from Pythagoras’ theorem. Page 3 Example 1 calculates squared distances by substitution before taking square roots. Page 4 repeats the squared-distance formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate squared side lengths and use the converse of Pythagoras’ theorem to establish a right angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two side lengths and use their equality to justify that the triangle is isosceles.

questions.mappingNote: Applying the distance formula to XY and XZ establishes two equal sides and hence an isosceles triangle. Neither supplied reuse candidate has the same complete task and coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Use the distance formula derived from Pythagoras, calculating squared lengths before taking positive square roots, as demonstrated in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two side lengths and use their equality to justify that the triangle is isosceles.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two midpoints and use their equality to establish mutual bisection.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught midpoint formula separately to AB and CD, then explain that their common midpoint establishes mutual bisection.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 derives the midpoint formula by averaging corresponding coordinates; page 4 Example 2 demonstrates substitution and exact coordinate arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two midpoints and use their equality to establish mutual bisection.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate four side lengths and use equal opposite sides to establish a parallelogram.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught distance formula to all four sides and conclude that the quadrilateral is a parallelogram because both pairs of opposite sides are equal.
questions.methodNote: Use squared coordinate differences to calculate each side's squared length, then take the square root, following the distance-formula derivation, Example 1 and the formula summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate four side lengths and use equal opposite sides to establish a parallelogram.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of integer coordinates into the gradient formula, including negative differences and a horizontal interval.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess the gradient formula demonstrated in Example 3. No line equation or parallel/perpendicular test is required.
questions.methodNote: Use gradient as rise divided by run, substituting coordinates consistently into m=(y2-y1)/(x2-x1), then simplify exactly. Page 7 Example 3 demonstrates signed subtraction and a three-line calculation; its horizontal-interval discussion establishes zero gradient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of integer coordinates into the gradient formula, including negative differences and a horizontal interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two gradients from coordinates and use their equality to establish parallel lines.

questions.mappingNote: Page 7 states the equal-gradient criterion for parallel lines. Example 4 on page 8 demonstrates the same two-coordinate-pairs proof required here.
questions.methodNote: Calculate each gradient as the change in y divided by the corresponding change in x. Equal gradients establish that the lines are parallel.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two gradients from coordinates and use their equality to establish parallel lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a given gradient and two points into the gradient formula, then solve for an unknown coordinate.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 defines and derives the gradient formula. Page 7 Example 3 demonstrates coordinate substitution and simplification. This question reverses that calculation to determine a missing y-coordinate.
questions.methodNote: Use gradient as rise divided by run, substituting corresponding coordinates consistently into m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), then solve the resulting equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a given gradient and two points into the gradient formula, then solve for an unknown coordinate.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a missing horizontal coordinate into the gradient formula and solve the resulting equation.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 defines gradient as the change in y divided by the change in x; Example 3 on page 7 demonstrates substitution with negative coordinates. The missing-coordinate task directly assesses application of that formula.
questions.methodNote: Use the gradient formula with the coordinates in consistent order, simplify signed differences, and solve for the missing coordinate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a missing horizontal coordinate into the gradient formula and solve the resulting equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate gradients and rearrange the gradient formula to recover missing coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 defines the gradient formula; Example 3 on page 7 demonstrates signed-coordinate substitutions. Question 5 applies this formula directly and inversely within a completion table.
questions.methodNote: Use gradient as rise divided by run, m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), retaining corresponding coordinate order. Substitute the missing coordinate as a variable and solve the resulting equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate gradients and rearrange the gradient formula to recover missing coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate two gradients from coordinates and use their product to establish perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: Page 8 states the perpendicular-gradient criterion. Example 5 and the summary on page 9 demonstrate exactly the two-gradient calculation and product test required by question 6.
questions.methodNote: Calculate each gradient using the difference of y-coordinates divided by the corresponding difference of x-coordinates. Establish perpendicularity by showing that their product is -1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate two gradients from coordinates and use their product to establish perpendicularity.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the perpendicular-gradient product rule directly to five given nonzero gradients.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 directly applies the perpendicular-gradient rule stated on page 8 and consolidated on page 9; no coordinate calculation or diagram is required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 establish that perpendicular non-axis-parallel lines have gradients whose product is −1. Solve the product equation for the unknown gradient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the perpendicular-gradient product rule directly to five given nonzero gradients.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate one gradient from coordinates, then use parallel and perpendicular sides of a rectangle to infer two further gradients.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 supplies the coordinate gradient formula; Example 3 on page 7 demonstrates substitution. Pages 7–8 establish equal gradients for parallel lines, while pages 8–9 and Example 5 establish the perpendicular-gradient product. These methods directly support parts a, b and c respectively.
questions.methodNote: Use rise divided by run to calculate gradient. Parallel sides have equal gradients; perpendicular sides have gradients whose product is -1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate one gradient from coordinates, then use parallel and perpendicular sides of a rectangle to infer two further gradients.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine plotting, opposite-side gradient comparisons and the diagonal-bisection property of a parallelogram.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 6–7 define and demonstrate gradients, including zero gradient for horizontal intervals. Page 8 Example 4 demonstrates proving parallelism by comparing gradients. Pages 3–4 derive and demonstrate midpoint coordinates. Question 9 integrates these methods with plotting and parallelogram properties, supporting the coordinate-geometry-problems classification.
questions.methodNote: Use the coordinate gradient formula, equal gradients for parallel lines, and the midpoint formula. Conclude that both pairs of opposite sides are parallel; then use the diagonal-bisection property of a parallelogram.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine plotting, opposite-side gradient comparisons and the diagonal-bisection property of a parallelogram.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose midpoint calculations followed by opposite-side gradient comparisons to prove a parallelogram; these are routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 3–4 teach the midpoint formula. Pages 6–9 teach the gradient formula and equal gradients for parallel lines, including the comparison in Example 4. This question combines those methods in a quadrilateral proof.
questions.methodNote: Find midpoints by averaging corresponding coordinates, calculate gradients using change in y divided by change in x, and use equal gradients to establish parallel opposite sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose midpoint calculations followed by opposite-side gradient comparisons to prove a parallelogram; these are routine linked procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine distance and gradient calculations with equal and parallel sides of a square.

questions.mappingNote: Example 1 on page 3 supplies the distance-working sequence. Example 3 on page 7 supplies gradient substitutions; pages 7–9 establish equal gradients for parallel lines.
questions.methodNote: Use the squared-distance calculation followed by its positive square root, calculate gradient from coordinate differences, and transfer the gradient to a parallel side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine distance and gradient calculations with equal and parallel sides of a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate and compare two gradients, including negative coordinates, to decide collinearity.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 6–7 define interval and line gradients and demonstrate negative-coordinate substitutions. The same-gradient property for intervals on one line directly supports the collinearity decisions.
questions.methodNote: Calculate each interval's gradient from corresponding coordinate differences and compare the results. Intervals sharing a point with the same gradient lie on the same line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate and compare two gradients, including negative coordinates, to decide collinearity.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a gradient, transfer it to the parallel opposite side, use equal directed coordinate changes to locate D, then apply the midpoint formula. The labelled diagram and explicit parts scaffold these routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 6–9 teach rise/run, coordinate gradients and parallel-line gradients. Pages 3–4 teach coordinate averaging for midpoints. Applying these to the supplied parallelogram assesses combined coordinate geometry.
questions.methodNote: Calculate gradient using coordinate differences; parallel opposite sides have equal gradients. Use equal directed horizontal and vertical changes along opposite sides to locate D, then average endpoint coordinates for each midpoint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a gradient, transfer it to the parallel opposite side, use equal directed coordinate changes to locate D, then apply the midpoint formula. The labelled diagram and explicit parts scaffold these routine linked procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the coefficient of x and the constant directly from equations already in gradient–intercept form.

questions.mappingNote: Every part is already in gradient–intercept form and requires interpretation rather than rearrangement. Page 12 Example 6 and the page 16 summary provide the directly applicable method.
questions.methodNote: Use y=mx+b, identifying m as the gradient and b as the y-intercept. Example 6b directly demonstrates reading both values from an equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the coefficient of x and the constant directly from equations already in gradient–intercept form.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of the supplied gradient and y-intercept into gradient–intercept form.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess writing an equation from a supplied gradient and y-intercept; general-form conversion is not required.
questions.methodNote: Use the gradient–intercept equation y=mx+b, substituting the given gradient for m and the given y-intercept for b, as demonstrated in Example 6a on printed page 112.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of the supplied gradient and y-intercept into gradient–intercept form.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught constant-coordinate line forms, isolate a variable in four one-step equations, and identify horizontal gradients as zero and vertical gradients as undefined.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve equations directly assess the horizontal/vertical line forms taught on page 12. Part m applies the same page's gradient distinction.
questions.methodNote: The Horizontal lines and Vertical lines sections identify y=b as horizontal with gradient zero and x=a as vertical with undefined gradient. Sketch each line through its corresponding axis intercept; isolate x or y first for parts i–l.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught constant-coordinate line forms, isolate a variable in four one-step equations, and identify horizontal gradients as zero and vertical gradients as undefined.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange linear equations into general form, clearing fractional coefficients where necessary.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess conversion into general form. Example 7 on PDF page 13 supplies the required method; pages 12 and 16 establish and summarise the equation forms.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 clears denominators by multiplying the entire equation, then collects all terms on one side to obtain ax+by+c=0. The accompanying explanation states that general form is not unique.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange linear equations into general form, clearing fractional coefficients where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose inverse operations to collect the y term and divide by its coefficient, converting each equation into the requested form; no additional insight is required.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses the rearrangement demonstrated in Example 8 on page 13; page 12 establishes gradient–intercept form.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 rearranges each equation to isolate the y term, then divides by its coefficient to obtain y=mx+b. Exact fractions are retained.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose inverse operations to collect the y term and divide by its coefficient, converting each equation into the requested form; no additional insight is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Link routine rearrangement into y=mx+b with interpreting the resulting x coefficient and constant as gradient and y-intercept.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts require the same taught conversion and interpretation. Parts a, c, d, e, g and h yield fractional gradients; b, f and i yield integer gradients. No intercept plotting or graphical solution is requested.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 on PDF page 13 isolates y and then identifies the gradient as its x coefficient and the y-intercept as the constant, using the gradient–intercept definition on page 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Link routine rearrangement into y=mx+b with interpreting the resulting x coefficient and constant as gradient and y-intercept.

classification.difficultyReason: Associate each requested axis intercept with setting the other coordinate to zero, then solve the resulting linear equation and distinguish the two intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses finding both axis intercepts; no graph is requested. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: Example 9a–d finds the x-intercept by substituting y=0 and the y-intercept by substituting x=0, then solves the resulting linear equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Associate each requested axis intercept with setting the other coordinate to zero, then solve the resulting linear equation and distinguish the two intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Find two intercepts and sketch familiar straight lines; variable fractions add arithmetic rather than a new method.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts require this intercept-first construction. Graphing the linear relationship is the final assessed task, with identifying intercepts supporting it. The point–gradient teaching beginning below Question 16 is outside Exercise 4C and is not used.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 teaches setting y=0 to find the x-intercept and x=0 to find the y-intercept, then drawing the line through those points. Example 9 on pages 14–15 demonstrates exact fractional intercepts and labelled coordinate sketches.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find both intercepts, including fractional intercepts, and use them to sketch each line.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise horizontal or vertical lines and use the corresponding coordinate of a given point.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses identifying a horizontal or vertical line from its parallel axis and selecting the fixed coordinate of the supplied point.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 teaches that a horizontal line through P(a,b) has equation y=b and a vertical line has equation x=a. Example 9e on pages 14–15 illustrates x=4 as a vertical line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise horizontal or vertical lines and use the corresponding coordinate of a given point.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal and vertical lines and lines through the origin using one additional point.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess sketching a line from its equation. Parts a and d use constant-coordinate lines; b, c, e and f use the origin and a convenient second point.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 identifies x=a as vertical and y=b as horizontal. Pages 14–15 teach sketching y=mx through the origin and a second point obtained by choosing a nonzero x-value; Example 9e demonstrates a vertical line and Example 9f demonstrates a line through the origin.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal and vertical lines and lines through the origin using one additional point.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a known coordinate into the supplied linear equation and solve for the missing coordinate.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess finding a missing coordinate by substitution into 3x−12y=30. None of the supplied reuse candidates has this complete stem, equation and set of six coordinate pairs.
questions.methodNote: Page 15, Example 10, substitutes each supplied coordinate directly into the line equation and solves for the pronumeral. Page 12 explains that coordinates of points on a line satisfy its equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a known coordinate into the supplied linear equation and solve for the missing coordinate.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the known coordinate, substitute into the supplied equation and evaluate or solve a short linear equation for the missing coordinate; the six parts repeat this direct method.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks for a missing coordinate of a point satisfying the given line, directly matching point-satisfies-line.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 explains that coordinates of points on a line satisfy its equation. Example 10 on page 15 substitutes the known coordinate and solves for the pronumeral, retaining intermediate algebra.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the known coordinate, substitute into the supplied equation and evaluate or solve a short linear equation for the missing coordinate; the six parts repeat this direct method.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute both given coordinates into y=-4x+c and isolate c using one multiplication and one addition.

questions.mappingNote: Question 13 applies the same substitution method to determine the constant c from a point known to lie on the line. The closest catalogue skill is point-satisfies-line.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 states that coordinates of points on a line satisfy its equation. Example 10 on page 15 substitutes known coordinates into the equation and solves for the remaining pronumeral.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute both given coordinates into y=-4x+c and isolate c using one multiplication and one addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a known point into a general-form equation and solve for an unknown coefficient, retaining the negative sign of the given ordinate.

questions.mappingNote: The same substitution method determines the unknown coefficient because the given point satisfies the equation. Recognising a point that satisfies a line is the closest existing catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 on PDF page 15 substitutes known coordinates into a line equation and solves the resulting linear equation, including substitution of a negative coordinate and exact fractional results.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a known point into a general-form equation and solve for an unknown coefficient, retaining the negative sign of the given ordinate.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange an equation containing an unknown coefficient and equate its gradient to the given value.

questions.mappingNote: Question 15 requires the same rearrangement with a symbolic coefficient, followed by equating a/3 to the given gradient 4. Point–gradient form is unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 identifies the coefficient of x in y=mx+b as the gradient. Example 8 on page 13 rearranges general-form equations into gradient–intercept form before identifying the gradient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange an equation containing an unknown coefficient and equate its gradient to the given value.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange an equation containing an unknown coefficient, identify its gradient and solve for that coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Question 16 requires the same rearrangement, followed by equating the coefficient 3/b to the supplied gradient and solving for b.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 identifies the coefficient of x in gradient–intercept form as the gradient. Example 8 on page 13 rearranges general-form equations to isolate y before reading off the gradient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange an equation containing an unknown coefficient, identify its gradient and solve for that coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the gradient of a parallel line, substitute the given point into point–gradient form and rearrange; recognise horizontal and vertical special cases.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c substitute the supplied gradient and point. Part d first identifies the common gradient -3. Part e substitutes gradient zero. Part f uses constant x for a vertical line. Point–gradient form is the principal assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 derives y-y₁=m(x-x₁). Example 11 on page 18 uses equal gradients for parallel lines, substitutes a point and expands to gradient–intercept or general form. Page 19 reiterates point–gradient form. Apply this sequence to a–e; recognise the vertical parallel line directly in f.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the gradient of a parallel line, substitute the given point into point–gradient form and rearrange; recognise horizontal and vertical special cases.

classification.difficultyReason: Find perpendicular gradients from equations in different forms, then use a given point to determine each line.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts apply Example 12 directly. Parts b and c first rearrange the supplied equation to identify its gradient. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks or givens.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 finds the negative reciprocal gradient and substitutes the given point into point–gradient form, then rearranges into general or gradient–intercept form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find perpendicular gradients from equations in different forms, then use a given point to determine each line.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine midpoint, gradient and point–gradient methods to determine a perpendicular bisector.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the midpoint formula, part b the gradient formula, part c point–gradient form, and part d combines the midpoint with a perpendicular gradient. The combined geometrical task maps to coordinate-geometry-problems.
questions.methodNote: Average corresponding coordinates for the midpoint; use change in y divided by change in x for gradient. Apply point–gradient form to a known point. For the perpendicular bisector, use the negative reciprocal gradient and the midpoint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine midpoint, gradient and point–gradient methods to determine a perpendicular bisector.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the gradient from given information, two points or a parallel line, then apply point–gradient form.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly apply point–gradient form; part c first calculates the gradient from the two supplied points; part d obtains the gradient from the parallel line. Finding the equation is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 derives point–gradient form. Example 11 on page 18 uses equal gradients for parallel lines, substitutes the given point and expands. Page 19 teaches finding the gradient from two points before using point–gradient form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the gradient from given information, two points or a parallel line, then apply point–gradient form.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate gradients from two points and use point–gradient form, recognising horizontal and vertical exceptions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c and f directly apply the two-point method. Part d has zero gradient; part e requires recognising the vertical line because its gradient is undefined.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 first calculates the gradient from the two points, then substitutes one point into point–gradient form and rearranges the equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate gradients from two points and use point–gradient form, recognising horizontal and vertical exceptions.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a line through two points and verify a third point by substitution to establish collinearity.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 explicitly requires finding the equation of AB and checking C. Point–gradient form is the main assessed method, supported by the gradient formula and substitution.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 and its summary find the gradient from two points, use point–gradient form with either point, and check point membership by substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a line through two points and verify a third point by substitution to establish collinearity.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine parallelogram properties with known line and distance formulas in scaffolded parts.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b use gradient then point–gradient form; c–d use parallel opposite sides; e uses the distance formula; f uses equal opposite sides. Their combination in a parallelogram supports coordinate-geometry-problems as the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 supply the squared-distance formula and exact surd simplification. Page 6 defines gradient from coordinate differences. Page 18 uses equal gradients for parallel lines, followed by point–gradient substitution. Page 19 explicitly finds a gradient from two points before applying point–gradient form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine line equations and distance calculations with equal gradients and equal opposite sides of a parallelogram.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the midpoints and gradients of a square's diagonals and use the product of gradients to establish perpendicularity.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 belongs to Exercise 4D before the 4E band. It combines midpoint and gradient calculations for the diagonals of a square, followed by the taught perpendicular-gradient test, so coordinate geometry problems is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 teach averaging corresponding coordinates to find a midpoint. Page 6 teaches gradient as change in y divided by change in x. Pages 8–9 teach that nonvertical lines are perpendicular when their gradients multiply to -1; Example 5 calculates both gradients and then their product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the midpoints and gradients of a square's diagonals and use the product of gradients to establish perpendicularity.

classification.difficultyReason: Link graphs of two familiar linear equations with their intersection, including exact fractional arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts require two line sketches and their common point; part c benefits from the exact-coordinate calculation used in Example 14.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 sketches lines from two points or intercepts. Example 14 plots both lines on one set of axes and equates their y-values to find exact intersection coordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch two lines and identify their intersection, including fractional coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute an explicit expression for one variable and solve, retaining exact fractional answers.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies a variable as subject; e equates two expressions for y and f retains the supplied fractional expression for x.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 substitutes the expression from one equation into the other, solves for one variable, substitutes back and checks both original equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute an explicit expression for one variable and solve, retaining exact fractional answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Select suitable equation multiples, eliminate one variable and substitute back, including fractional solutions.
